title: The apolipoprotein A-I mimetic peptide 4F prevents defects in vascular function in endotoxemic rats.
abstract: High density lipoprotein (HDL) and apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I) reduce inflammatory responses to lipopolysaccharide (LPS). We tested the hypothesis that the apoA-I mimetic peptide 4F prevents LPS-induced defects in blood pressure and vascular reactivity. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured in rats at baseline and 6 h after injection of LPS (10 mg/kg) or saline vehicle. Subgroups of LPS-treated rats also received 4F (10 mg/kg) or scrambled 4F (Sc-4F). LPS administration reduced SBP by 35% compared with baseline. 4F attenuated the reduction in SBP in LPS-treated rats (17% reduction), while Sc-4F was without effect. Ex vivo studies showed a reduced contractile response to phenylephrine (PE) in aortae of LPS-treated rats (ED(50) = 459 +/- 83 nM) compared with controls (ED(50) = 57 +/- 6 nM). This was associated with nitric oxide synthase 2 (NOS2) upregulation. 4F administration improved vascular contractility (ED(50) = 60 +/- 9 nM), reduced aortic NOS2 protein, normalized plasma levels of NO metabolites, and reduced mortality in LPS-treated rats. These changes were associated with a reduction in plasma endotoxin activity. In vivo administration of (14)C-4F and Bodipy-LPS resulted in their colocalization and retention in the HDL fraction. It is proposed that 4F promotes the localization of LPS to the HDL fraction, resulting in endotoxin neutralization. 4F may thus prevent LPS-induced hemodynamic changes associated with NOS2 induction.

We tested the hypothesis that the apoA-I mimetic peptide 4F prevents LPS-induced defects in blood pressure and vascular reactivity. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) was measured in rats at baseline and 6 h after injection of LPS (10 mg/kg) or saline vehicle.

title: Relative effects of telmisartan, candesartan and losartan on alleviating arterial stiffness in patients with hypertension complicated by diabetes mellitus: an evaluation using the cardio-ankle vascular index (CAVI).
abstract: Using the cardio-ankle vascular index (CAVI) as an indicator, we assessed improvement of arterial stiffness in 95 outpatients with hypertension complicated by type 2 diabetes mellitus who were treated orally for >or= 12 months with telmisartan 40 mg/day, losartan 50 mg/day or candesartan 8 mg/day. At 1 year, in the telmisartan and losartan groups CAVI did not change whereas in the candesartan group CAVI showed a statistically significant decrease of 2.70%. Although telmisartan is believed to enhance the activity of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR-gamma) in vitro, it did not ameliorate arterial stiffness in our patients. Candesartan, however, improved arterial stiffness independently of blood pressure lowering and without PPAR-gamma agonist action, possibly by direct action resulting from its potent affinity and binding capacity for the angiotensin II type 1 receptor. We conclude that candesartan is a potentially useful therapy against arterial stiffness in hypertensive patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

title: Altered vascular function in young women with polycystic ovary syndrome.
abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is characterized by hyperinsulinemic insulin resistance, a metabolic disorder that in other circumstances is associated with increased cardiovascular risk. We compared macrovascular and microvascular function in 19 women with PCOS with 12 control subjects matched as a group for body mass index. Macrovascular function was assessed by recording pulse wave velocity (PWV) across the aorta and brachial artery. Microvascular function was studied by wire myography, by measuring the concentration response curve to norepinephrine (NE) before and after incubation with insulin (100 and 1,000 pM). PWV at the level of the brachial artery was found to be significantly elevated in the PCOS group [9.08 (range, 8.34-11.15) m/sec(-1) vs. 8.27 (range, 7.5-9.01) m/sec(-1); P = 0.03]. In contrast, PWV measured in the aorta did not differ between the two groups [7.49 +/- 1.21 vs. 7.84 +/- 1.44 m/sec(-1); P = 0.8]. In vessels from control subjects, insulin reduced the contraction response to NE. At an insulin concentration of 100 pM, NE negative log EC50 (pD(2)) was 6.2 +/- 0.24 vs. 6.7 +/- 0.15 (P = 0.02). At a concentration of 1,000 pM, NE pD(2) was 6.4 +/- 0.14 vs. 6.9 +/- 0.19 (P = 0.0006). Both concentrations also caused attenuation in maximal tension developed in response to NE (insulin 100 pM, 12 +/- 3%, P = 0.002; insulin 1,000 pM, 17 +/- 5%, P = 0.009). In contrast, there was no change in the PCOS group with insulin at 100 pM for either pD(2) (6.7 +/- 0.24 vs. 6.8 +/- 0.27; P = 0.3) or maximum contraction (-0.4 +/- 2%; P = 0.8). At 1,000 pM, there was a change in pD(2) (6.4 +/- 0.2 vs. 6.8 +/- 0.2; P = 0.003) but not maximum contraction (4 +/- 3%; P = 0.2). In conclusion, this study is the first to demonstrate increased vascular stiffness and a functional defect in the vascular action of insulin ex vivo in patients with PCOS. We suggest that these findings are indicative of insulin resistance at a vascular level in women without overt cardiovascular disease.

We compared macrovascular and microvascular function in 19 women with PCOS with 12 control subjects matched as a group for body mass index. Macrovascular function was assessed by recording pulse wave velocity (PWV) across the aorta and brachial artery.

title: Mechanotransduction in Liver Fibrosis: Sinusoidal Remodeling, Mechanometabolic Coupling, and Therapeutic Implications.
abstract: Liver fibrosis has traditionally been interpreted through biochemical pathways driven by chronic injury, inflammation, metabolic stress, and profibrotic cytokine signaling. However, fibrotic progression also involves mechanical remodeling of the hepatic microenvironment. This review examines mechanotransduction in liver fibrosis, with particular emphasis on the sinusoidal niche as a mechanically responsive interface. During chronic liver injury, liver sinusoidal endothelial cell defenestration, altered shear stress, extracellular matrix deposition, and remodeling of the space of Disse modify the physical environment encountered by hepatocytes, hepatic stellate cells, macrophages, and endothelial cells. These changes are transmitted through integrins, focal adhesions, Rho-ROCK-dependent cytoskeletal tension, YAP/TAZ and MRTF-A/SRF signaling, mechanosensitive ion channels, and nuclear mechanotransduction, linking matrix mechanics to fibrogenic transcription, vascular dysfunction, and tissue stiffening. Specifically, in MASLD/MASH, lipid droplet expansion, hepatocyte nuclear deformation, perisinusoidal micro-stiffness, sinusoidal distortion, and increased intrahepatic resistance provide a disease-specific example of metabolic-mechanical coupling. MetALD/ALD add a membrane-level dimension, as alcohol exposure produces compartment-specific remodeling of plasma and organelle membranes and disrupts hepatocyte-extracellular matrix coupling. However, a direct membrane-fluidity-to-fibrosis pathway remains unproven. Clinically, vibration-controlled transient elastography and magnetic resonance elastography translate tissue-level mechanical changes into measurable information for fibrosis staging, monitoring, and risk stratification. This perspective also broadens antifibrotic strategies beyond collagen accumulation to include matrix cross-linking, cell-matrix mechanosensing, cytoskeletal contractility, nuclear mechanotransduction, and sinusoidal dysfunction. By integrating sinusoidal mechanics, cellular force transmission, clinical stiffness assessment, and therapeutic development, this review provides a mechanobiological framework to understand liver fibrosis and refine antifibrotic strategies.

However, fibrotic progression also involves mechanical remodeling of the hepatic microenvironment. This review examines mechanotransduction in liver fibrosis, with particular emphasis on the sinusoidal niche as a mechanically responsive interface.

title: Association between Brachial-Ankle Pulse Wave Velocity and Large-Nerve Fiber Function in Chinese Adults Aged 18-65 Years with Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Arterial stiffness, measured by brachial-ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV), has been linked to diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN). However, the evidence regarding its association with large-nerve fiber dysfunction, specifically assessed by vibration perception threshold (VPT), in Chinese patients aged 18-65 years with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is scarce. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between baPWV and VPT in this specific population.

METHODS: This cross-sectional study enrolled 600 inpatients with T2DM aged 18-65 years. baPWV was measured using an automated waveform analyzer. DPN was defined as a VPT ≥15 volts in at least one foot. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to assess independent association, expressed as odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Restricted cubic spline and subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the dose-response relationship and consistency of the association.

RESULTS: Among the participants, 165 (27.5%) were classified into the abnormal VPT group. After full adjustment for confounders including age, gender, diabetes duration, glycated hemoglobin, and lifestyle factors, each 100 cm/s increase in baPWV was significantly associated with increased odds of DPN (OR = 1.07, 95% CI: 1.01-1.14). When analyzed by quartiles, participants in the highest baPWV quartile (≥1,660 cm/s) had 1.29-fold higher odds of abnormal VPT (OR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.03-3.01) compared to those in the lowest quartile (<1,380 cm/s), with a significant trend across quartiles (p for trend = 0.005). A linear dose-response relationship was confirmed without evidence of a threshold effect. Subgroup analyses showed the association was consistent across different patient characteristics.

CONCLUSION: Elevated baPWV is independently associated with higher odds of DPN measured by VPT in Chinese patients aged 18-65 years with type 2 diabetes. This linear relationship not only underscores the pivotal role of arterial stiffness in the pathogenesis of DPN but also positions baPWV as a valuable tool for early risk stratification in clinical practice.

However, the evidence regarding its association with large-nerve fiber dysfunction, specifically assessed by vibration perception threshold (VPT), in Chinese patients aged 18-65 years with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is scarce. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between baPWV and VPT in this specific population.

title: Imaging the ex-vivo human cochlea using 1.3-μm and 1.7-μm optical coherence tomography.
abstract:
SIGNIFICANCE: There is no clinical imaging method to visualize the soft tissues of the human cochlea, which are crucial for sound transduction and are damaged in sensorineural hearing loss. Although optical coherence tomography (OCT) has been effective in small animal models, we show for the first time that it can image through the full thickness of the ex-vivo human otic capsule and resolve cochlear microstructures despite increased scattering.

AIM: We aim to investigate whether OCT could image the cochlea through the otic capsule. We compared 1.7 and 1.3 μ m OCT to test if the reduced scattering at 1.7 μ m provided any appreciable advantage for imaging the cochleae.

APPROACH: OCT interferometers were built for both 1.3 and 1.7 μ m wavelengths, using identical sample and reference arm optics in both systems. Imaging was performed on two fixed human temporal bones with intact cochleae. The interferometers were designed to allow seamless switching between 1.3 and 1.7 μ m OCT without disrupting the temporal bone during imaging.

RESULTS: We took volumetric OCT images at the base, apex, and hook regions of fixed ex-vivo human cochleae and compared the images taken at 1.3 μ m with those taken at 1.7 μ m . At both wavelengths, we could see through the otic capsule and identify cochlear structures. In some cases, 1.7 μ m OCT resulted in clearer images of the lateral wall, interior scala, and fine cochlear structures due to reduced multiple scattering at depth compared with 1.3 μ m .

CONCLUSIONS: We conclude that both 1.7 μ m and 1.3 μ m OCT can image through the human otic capsule, offering the potential for direct measurement of cochlear vibrometry or blood flow in living humans. Using 1.7 μ m light, we observed reduced multiple scattering in the otic capsule, leading to enhanced contrast of cochlear structures compared with 1.3 μ m . However, these improvements were marginal and came with trade-offs.

Although optical coherence tomography (OCT) has been effective in small animal models, we show for the first time that it can image through the full thickness of the ex-vivo human otic capsule and resolve cochlear microstructures despite increased scattering. AIM: We aim to investigate whether OCT could image the cochlea through the otic capsule.

title: Optimization of Synthetic Vocal Fold Models for Glottal Closure.
abstract: Synthetic, self-oscillating models of the human vocal folds are used to study the complex and inter-related flow, structure, and acoustical aspects of voice production. The vocal folds typically collide during each cycle, thereby creating a brief period of glottal closure that has important implications for flow, acoustic, and motion-related outcomes. Many previous synthetic models, however, have been limited by incomplete glottal closure during vibration. In this study, a low-fidelity, two-dimensional, multilayer finite element model of vocal fold flow-induced vibration was coupled with a custom genetic algorithm optimization code to determine geometric and material characteristics that would be expected to yield physiologically-realistic frequency and closed quotient values. The optimization process yielded computational models that vibrated with favorable frequency and closed quotient characteristics. A tradeoff was observed between frequency and closed quotient. A synthetic, self-oscillating vocal fold model with geometric and material properties informed by the simulation outcomes was fabricated and tested for onset pressure, oscillation frequency, and closed quotient. The synthetic model successfully vibrated at a realistic frequency and exhibited a nonzero closed quotient. The methodology described in this study provides potential direction for fabricating synthetic models using isotropic silicone materials that can be designed to vibrate with physiologically-realistic frequencies and closed quotient values. The results also show the potential for a low-fidelity model optimization approach to be used to tune synthetic vocal fold model characteristics for specific vibratory outcomes.

title: Placental abnormalities in congenital diaphragmatic hernia: A systematic review of experimental and clinical studies.
abstract: The placenta is essential for fetal organ development, and its dysfunction is implicated in several congenital anomalies. However, little is known about the status and role of the placenta in congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Herein, we aimed to define the incidence of placental abnormalities in CDH and characterize gross morphology, histology, molecular pathways, and vascular function. Using a predefined search strategy, we performed a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines. Human and animal studies reporting on placental and/or umbilical cord abnormalities in CDH were analyzed. Of 2,820 records identified, 14 articles were included. Human studies reported no consistent macroscopic placental phenotype. Cord abnormalities included hypercoiling, abnormal insertion, and single umbilical artery. Fetal vascular malperfusion, thrombotic lesions, and chronic inflammation were reported at histology. Ex-vivo CDH fetoplacental arteries showed impaired function with excessive constriction and inadequate relaxation. Animal studies reported reduced placental weight, trophoblast injury and apoptosis, and altered retinoid metabolism. Despite extensive literature on CDH, the status of the placenta remains understudied. Available evidence indicates that CDH is associated with abnormalities involving fetal placental vascular pathology. Studies using standardized assessment are needed to define the role of the placenta in CDH and correlate its status with disease severity and neonatal outcomes.

However, little is known about the status and role of the placenta in congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). title: Human foetal cortical slice cultures: A translational platform for studying early neurodevelopment.
abstract: The developing human neocortex is characterised by complex and dynamic changes in cellular architecture, neuronal organisation and activity. We previously described how human foetal cortical organotypic slice cultures, prepared from ethically sourced tissue could be used to investigate these processes. Cultures can be maintained for weeks, exhibiting features of the normal developing brain that are not replicated in current organoid models. Such cultures allow the possibility for experimental manipulation, for instance testing the effects of genetic mutations. Here we extend the characterisation of our model. We report that these organotypic cultures preserve the laminar organisation of the developing cortical wall and show considerable diversity of neuronal morphology. Employing bulk mRNA hybridisation for 794 genes (a "human neuropathology" gene panel), we identified consistent patterns of evolving gene expression between 0 and 14 days in vitro (DIV) across different tissue samples taken at 16-18 post-conceptional weeks (pcw). To put this in the context of the normal developmental pattern, we compared our data set with previously acquired tissue RNAseq data collected between 7-17 pcw (https://www.hdbr.org/expression). This indicated that many gene expression changes in vitro followed prior developmental trajectories, but others diverged strongly, including upregulated genes associated with responses to stress, and downregulated genes associated with the vascular function. This latter effect may reflect the redundancy of vascular development in culture. Notably, various genes associated with pre- and post- synaptic function, including both glutamate and GABA receptors, continued to be expressed strongly. Consistent with this, we observed spontaneous neuronal network activity in the subplate (SP) using targeted expression of the genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator, GCaMPf6, to post-mitotic neurons. The frequency of neuronal Ca2+ transients increased when blockers of either GABAA receptors or gap junctions were applied. Conversely, activity was significantly reduced by glutamatergic receptor antagonists and abolished by voltage gated sodium channel blockade. Neuronal Ca2+ transients were triggered directly by focal application of glutamate in the SP and subventricular zone, whereas cortical plate neurons exhibited weaker responses. This was consistent with levels of immunoreactivity for glutamate receptor sub-units in these compartments. In conclusion, the organotypic cultures show functional synaptic networks, supported by continued expression of the relevant synaptic protein machinery. These data provide further validation of organotypic cultures as a model for investigating and manipulating the early prenatal development of human neocortex, a period that is otherwise difficult to study.

title: Prenatal melatonin regulates lung prostanoids expression in newborn sheep exposed to chronic hypoxia.
abstract: Chronic hypoxia during pregnancy disrupts the balance of pulmonary vasoactive agents, altering prostanoid signaling and increasing the contractility of resistance arteries. This leads to elevated pulmonary arterial pressure and vascular resistance, ultimately resulting in pulmonary hypertension of the neonate (PHN). While prenatal melatonin is known to influence vascular tone, its specific impact on the neonatal pulmonary prostanoid system in hypoxic pregnancies remains unclear. This study aimed to determine the effects of third-trimester maternal melatonin administration on the cyclooxygenase and prostanoid pathways, and to evaluate its efficacy in reversing PHN in a high-altitude ovine model. In-vivo and ex-vivo pulmonary vascular function was evaluated in neonatal lambs gestated and born under chronic hypoxia. Furthermore, lung samples from 12-day-old lambs were analyzed using RT-PCR, Western blotting, and immunohistochemistry. The results demonstrate that prenatal melatonin actively modulates the pulmonary vascular function, and the prostanoids system, altering both the transcriptional and translational expression of specific prostanoids, as well as their spatial localization within pulmonary resistance arteries. However, despite this significant molecular and structural modulation, maternal melatonin treatment failed to reverse or clinically improve PHN in the offspring. These findings highlight the complexity of hypoxia-induced vascular remodeling and suggest that melatonin-driven prostanoid modulation alone is insufficient to overcome PHN, although it can improve some pulmonary function in neonates.
englishSummary: Chronic hypoxia during pregnancy disrupts the balance of pulmonary vasoactive agents, altering prostanoid signaling and increasing the contractility of resistance arteries. This leads to elevated pulmonary arterial pressure and vascular resistance, ultimately resulting in pulmonary hypertension of the neonate (PHN). title: High-fat diet disrupts retinal vessel reactivity and redox balance.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: A high-fat diet (HFD) is a major public health concern associated with vascular dysfunction and systemic pathological alterations, often linked to oxidative stress and redox imbalance. However, its effects on the retinal microvasculature remain incompletely understood.

OBJECTIVE: This study tested the hypothesis that prolonged HFD exposure induces endothelial dysfunction in retinal arterioles.

METHODS: Mice were fed an HFD for 18 weeks, while age-matched controls received a normal chow diet. Retinal arteriole reactivity to changes in intraluminal pressure and vasoactive agents was assessed in vitro. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production was quantified in retinal cryosections using dihydroethidium staining. Expression of redox- and inflammation-related genes was analyzed in retinal explants by quantitative real-time PCR. Protein expression of key signaling molecules was evaluated by immunofluorescence microscopy.

RESULTS: Retinal arterioles from HFD-fed mice exhibited attenuated responses to increased intraluminal pressure and impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation to acetylcholine. ROS levels were elevated in retinal tissue following HFD exposure. Gene expression analysis revealed upregulation of hypoxia- and redox-related markers, including HIF-1α, VEGF-A, and NOX2, as well as the proinflammatory cytokine TNF-α and antioxidant enzyme catalase. Immunofluorescence staining demonstrated increased expression of the receptor for advanced glycation endproducts (RAGE) and NOX2.

CONCLUSION: Chronic HFD exposure induces endothelial dysfunction in the retinal microvasculature, associated with increased oxidative stress and altered redox signaling. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the impact of diet-induced metabolic stress on retinal vascular function.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: A high-fat diet (HFD) is a major public health concern associated with vascular dysfunction and systemic pathological alterations, often linked to oxidative stress and redox imbalance. However, its effects on the retinal microvasculature remain incompletely understood. OBJECTIVE: This study tested the hypothesis that prolonged HFD exposure induces endothelial dysfunction in retinal arterioles.

title: Vascular Abnormalities in the Hand and Wrist: State-of-the-Art Multimodality Imaging.
abstract: Vascular abnormalities are less common in the hand and wrist than in the lower extremities but can result in significant morbidity if unrecognized or untreated. The unique vascular architecture of the hand and wrist, with a dense network of arterial anastomoses, confers resilience to ischemia, but the superficial location makes them vulnerable to trauma and occupational injury. The authors describe and illustrate a comprehensive multimodality imaging approach to the diagnosis and evaluation of vascular abnormalities of the hand and wrist. They begin with an overview of vascular anatomy and normal variants, including a persistent median artery. Multimodality imaging, including US, CT angiography, MR angiography, and digital subtraction angiography, is reviewed with a focus on strengths, limitations, and clinical utility. Dynamic imaging techniques and photon-counting CT are highlighted for their evolving roles. A wide spectrum of vascular diseases, including atherosclerosis, trauma, iatrogenic injury, embolism, hypothenar hammer syndrome, hand-arm vibration syndrome, vasculitis, and frostbite, as well as their imaging appearances, are discussed. Vascular anomalies, including vascular malformations and vascular neoplasms, are also reviewed. The role of imaging in hand transplantation is addressed. The authors provide a framework for recognizing vascular diseases in the hand and wrist and selecting the appropriate imaging modality. Familiarity with vascular anatomy, imaging findings, and clinical context is essential for timely diagnosis, guiding management, and preserving limb function.

title: Endohepatology in the Management of Portal Hypertension in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease.
abstract: Portal hypertension is the principal driver of decompensation in advanced chronic liver disease, yet in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) it deviates from the classical sinusoidal paradigm. Growing evidence points to a mixed sinusoidal-presinusoidal phenotype in which the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) may underestimate true portal pressure, and in which decompensation and varices can occur at lower HVPG values than in viral cirrhosis. This biology is compounded by a diagnostic gap: non-invasive tests such as liver stiffness by vibration-controlled transient elastography, FIB-4, ANTICIPATE-NASH, spleen stiffness and the NICER model, are degraded by obesity through technical limitations and altered diagnostic thresholds, even when test discrimination is preserved. Moreover, no non-invasive rule-in for clinically significant portal hypertension reaches a 90% positive predictive value in obese MASLD, leaving a clinically meaningful grey zone. Endohepatology addresses these diagnostic limitations by providing complementary hemodynamic, elastographic, and histological information. Within a single sedated session, EUS-guided shear-wave elastography and EUS-guided liver biopsy can adjudicate F2-F3 fibrosis when treatment eligibility is uncertain; EUS-guided portal pressure gradient measurement can provide a direct gradient when HVPG or non-invasive tests are discordant with the clinical phenotype; and EUS-based vascular assessment can characterize collateral and variceal anatomy. The same platform extends to therapy, including EUS-guided gastric variceal obliteration and pre-bariatric risk stratification. Current evidence is largely early-phase and requires prospective validation. Rather than replacing established tools, endohepatology offers an integrated pathway tailored to the diagnostic and therapeutic problems most characteristic of MASLD.

title: Citrulline Supplementation Improves Aortic Vasodilation and Prevents Aortic Thickening Only in Female Rats.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Aging is associated with endothelial dysfunction and vascular remodeling, partly due to reduced nitric oxide (NO) bioavailability. l-citrulline, a precursor of l-arginine and NO synthesis, has been proposed as a therapeutic strategy to improve vascular function. This study evaluated the effects of chronic citrulline supplementation on aortic structure and vasodilatory function in adult male and female rats.

METHODS: Eight-month-old male and female Sprague-Dawley rats were randomly assigned to control or treatment groups. The treated animals received oral malate citrulline (1 g/kg/d) for 12 weeks. We isolated thoracic aortas for histological and morphometric analyses, including tunica media thickness and intima/media ratio. We assessed vascular reactivity in vitro using isolated aortic rings in an organ bath system, measuring acetylcholine (ACh)-induced relaxation following phenylephrine-induced contraction.

RESULTS: Citrulline supplementation significantly improved ACh-induced vasorelaxation in female rats compared with female controls (55.14% ± 4.8% vs 42.4% ± 4.3%, P < .05. No differences in vasorelaxation were observed in males between the treated and control groups. Histological analyses showed that treated females had less disruption of elastic fibers and a thinner minimal intima than controls, whereas males showed no structural differences.

CONCLUSIONS: Citrulline supplementation improves endothelium-dependent vasodilation and may preserve aortic structural integrity in female rats but not in males. These findings suggest a sex-dependent vascular response to citrulline, potentially mediated by differences in NO signaling and hormonal regulation. Citrulline may represent a therapeutic strategy to improve vascular function during aging, particularly in females.

CLINICAL IMPACT: The findings may guide clinical trials investigating how hormonal status and nitric oxide signaling affect the efficacy of citrulline supplementation in female patients. Ultimately, these insights could establish citrulline as a targeted, preventive intervention to preserve aortic structural integrity and reduce cardiovascular disease risk in the aging female population.

This study evaluated the effects of chronic citrulline supplementation on aortic structure and vasodilatory function in adult male and female rats.

title: Transcription factor EB as a novel target for dimethyl fumarate to restore endothelial function in diabetes.
abstract: Diabetes mellitus-associated endothelial dysfunction represents a pivotal early event in diabetic vasculopathy, linking metabolic derangements to vascular injury. Dimethyl fumarate (DMF), an FDA-approved drug for multiple sclerosis and psoriasis, exhibits potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, yet whether it protects against diabetic endothelial dysfunction and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, diabetic db/db mice and the non-diabetic db/m+ littermates were treated with DMF (100 mg·kg-1·d-1) or vehicle for 4 weeks, and vascular function in aortic and mesenteric artery rings was assessed by wire myography. Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) and endothelial cell (EC)-specific Tfeb knockout (TfebECKO) mice were employed to investigate the target of DMF in vitro and in vivo. DMF restored the impaired endothelium-dependent relaxations (EDRs) in db/db mouse aortas and insulin-induced relaxations in mesenteric arteries, improved glucose tolerance, reduced aortic endothelial mitochondrial ROS (mito-ROS) accumulation, and lowered the expression of inflammatory markers. IL-1β induced phosphorylation and cytoplasmic retention of TFEB (indicative of TFEB inhibition), mito-ROS production, and inflammatory responses in HUVECs and mouse aortas, all of which were reversed by DMF pretreatment. These protective effects of DMF were largely reversed by TFEB knockdown in HUVECs or in aortas of TfebECKO mice. RNA sequencing data analysis revealed a substantial overlap between DMF-regulated and TFEB-overexpression transcriptional profiles, implicating a role of TFEB in DMF-induced suppression of inflammatory and oxidative pathways. Together, DMF ameliorates endothelial dysfunction in diabetes by inhibiting TFEB phosphorylation and restoring TFEB nuclear activity. Endothelial TFEB represents a critical mediator responsible for the vaso-protective effects of DMF and a promising therapeutic target for the treatment of diabetic vascular complications.

title: Sex dimorphism in vascular trajectories after living-donor kidney transplantation: a prospective exploratory cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular risk remains high after kidney transplantation, reflecting pre-transplant early vascular aging. Arterial stiffness generally improves, but the trajectory of microvascular endothelial function, and its dependence on recipient's biological sex and donor matching, is unclear.

METHODS: In 71 living-donor kidney transplant recipients, microvascular endothelial function (reactive hyperemia index, lnRHI) and arterial stiffness [augmentation index at 75 bpm (AI@75)] were measured before transplantation and at a median of 24.6 months. Forty-six of their donors were assessed identically before donation, providing a healthy reference of the same sex. Resistance arteries from 37 recipients and 46 living donors underwent wire myography.

RESULTS: AI@75 improved overall (-5.7%; P = .003), whereas microvascular function declined in men but not women (male ΔlnRHI -0.149, P = .002; sex × time interaction β = -0.19, P = .026), stable in direction across 11 specifications including tacrolimus exposure and graft function. The greater AI@75 improvement with sex-matched transplantation (P = .020) did not survive adjustment for baseline stiffness (P = .32). Ex vivo, endothelial relaxation showed no detectable sex difference in recipients (P = .83) or donors (P = .94), whereas passive stiffness was higher in female recipients (P = .048).

CONCLUSIONS: After living-donor kidney transplantation, arterial stiffness improved in both sexes, while microvascular endothelial function declined in men and not in women. Referenced to healthy donors of the same sex, arterial stiffness in men remained abnormal at follow-up. Sex-matched transplantation conferred no independent vascular benefit. These findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger cohorts.

Arterial stiffness generally improves, but the trajectory of microvascular endothelial function, and its dependence on recipient's biological sex and donor matching, is unclear. METHODS: In 71 living-donor kidney transplant recipients, microvascular endothelial function (reactive hyperemia index, lnRHI) and arterial stiffness [augmentation index at 75 bpm (AI@75)] were measured before transplantation and at a median of 24.6 months.

title: Elastography and Vector Flow Imaging Detect Arteriovenous Fistula Stenosis Independent of Luminal Diameter.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To evaluate the diagnostic value of multimodal ultrasound (US)-including 2-dimensional (2D) US, sound touch elastography (STE), and vector flow imaging (VFI)-for the identification of functional and biomechanical abnormalities indicative of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) stenosis or occlusion in hemodialysis patients.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective study enrolled 37 hemodialysis patients with AVFs, divided into normal (n = 20) and dysfunction (n = 17) groups based on digital subtraction angiography (DSA) or clinical/US criteria. For the dysfunction group, AVF stenosis was defined as >50% luminal diameter reduction on DSA, and occlusion was defined as complete absence of flow. For the normal group, dysfunction was excluded by clinical examination (thrill/bruit) and normal duplex parameters. All patients underwent 2D US, STE, and VFI examinations. Key parameters measured included vessel diameter, elasticity (kPa), blood flow velocities, turbulence (Tur) index, and wall shear stress (WSS). Statistical comparisons were made between groups.

RESULTS: No significant differences were found in vessel diameter or intima status between groups. However, the stenosis/occlusion group exhibited significantly lower mean blood flow, peak systolic/end-diastolic velocities, and WSS, along with higher resistance index and vessel wall stiffness (STE mean, 30.35 kPa [SD ± 11.65] vs 20.7 kPa [SD ± 7.52]; P < .01). VFI revealed reduced blood flow velocity, Tur, and WSS in dysfunctional AVFs (all P < .01).

CONCLUSIONS: Multimodal US integrating 2D US, STE, and VFI provides a comprehensive assessment of AVF structure and function, detecting functional and biomechanical abnormalities associated with AVF stenosis or occlusion.
englishSummary: PURPOSE: To evaluate the diagnostic value of multimodal ultrasound (US)-including 2-dimensional (2D) US, sound touch elastography (STE), and vector flow imaging (VFI)-for the identification of functional and biomechanical abnormalities indicative of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) stenosis or occlusion in hemodialysis patients. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This prospective study enrolled 37 hemodialysis patients with AVFs, divided into normal (n = 20) and dysfunction (n = 17) groups based on digital subtraction angiography (DSA) or clinical/US criteria. For the dysfunction group, AVF stenosis was defined as >50% luminal diameter reduction on DSA, and occlusion was defined as complete absence of flow.

title: Uncovering the transcriptional hallmarks of endothelial cell aging via integrated single-cell analysis.
abstract: Endothelial cells (ECs) are critical regulators of vascular function and exhibit tissue-specialized roles. During aging, these cells become dysfunctional, resulting in increased susceptibility to cardiovascular disease. Although single-cell transcriptomics has revealed extensive endothelial heterogeneity, a comprehensive atlas of human EC transcriptomes over the course of the adult human lifespan has been lacking. Here, we present the Human Aging Endothelial Cell Atlas (HAECA), a harmonized single-cell transcriptomic compendium of over 375,000 ECs from 12 human tissues throughout adulthood. We identified age-associated transcriptional shifts, including a decline in angiogenic gene expression in venous ECs and widespread alterations in extracellular matrix and mechanotransduction-associated signatures. Furthermore, we uncovered a p21-linked transcriptional program in ECs, which we linked to cellular senescence in both in vitro and in vivo models. Together, our study provides a high-resolution transcriptomic reference of the human endothelium across tissues and age.

title: Beyond Hereditary Haemorrhagic Telangiectasia (HHT): Capillary Malformation-Arteriovenous Syndrome (CM-AVM).
abstract:
PRESENTATION: A woman in her forties, asymptomatic, was referred to the respiratory clinic with suspected HHT due to mucocutaneous telangiectasia involving her face, lips, and hands. Auscultation revealed an audible bruit over her left posterior chest wall.

DIAGNOSIS: MRI brain and spine showed no evidence of cerebral arteriovenous malformations. Genetic testing identified a heterozygous EPHB4 splice variant consistent with CM-AVM syndrome. It was negative for mutations associated with HHT.

TREATMENT: Red flags indicating pulmonary, intracranial or spinal haemorrhage were explained to the patient. She was linked in with the HHT clinic for routine follow-up and received genetic counselling.

DISCUSSION: CM-AVM is a rare autosomal dominant vascular malformation syndrome that can clinically mimic HHT but is genetically and phenotypically distinct. It should be considered in patients presenting with mucocutaneous vascular lesions. Genetic testing is essential to guide appropriate surveillance, management, and genetic counselling.

Auscultation revealed an audible bruit over her left posterior chest wall. DIAGNOSIS: MRI brain and spine showed no evidence of cerebral arteriovenous malformations.

title: Endovascular salvage of dysfunctional native haemodialysis arteriovenous fistulas: Clinical outcomes and predictors of patency.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypofunctioning haemodialysis arteriovenous fistulas are an important cause of inadequate dialysis, access failure and morbidity in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), and timely catheter-based intervention may help restore access function and prolong fistula usability.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy, feasibility, and safety of catheter-based interventional procedures for hypofunctioning haemodialysis fistulas in patients with CKD.

METHODS: This single-centre, retrospective observational follow up study, enrolled with 100 CKD patients on maintenance haemodialysis with dysfunctional native arteriovenous fistulas who underwent fistulogram and catheter-based intervention.

RESULTS: The mean age was 57.2 ± 12.4 years, 62.0% were male, Hypertension (80.0%) and diabetes mellitus (57.0%) were the major comorbidities. Radio cephalic fistula was the commonest access type (46.0%), and inadequate dialysis was the leading presentation (73.0%). Fistulography showed significant stenosis in 96.0%, with central vein involvement in 43.0% and long-segment lesions in 56.0%. Angioplasty was attempted in 96.0%, achieving technical success in 91.7% of attempted interventions and clinical success in 85.0%. Stenosis and pressure gradient reduced significantly after intervention (both p < 0.001). Complications occurred in 13.0%, with no deaths. Primary patency declined from 82.0% at 1 month to 58.0% at 6 months and 38.0% at 12 months. Patency loss was independently predicted by older age, central vein lesions, long lesions, residual stenosis, and absent post-procedure thrill.

CONCLUSION: Catheter-based endovascular intervention may be an effective fistula-salvage strategy for hypofunctioning haemodialysis arteriovenous fistulas, although long-term patency was influenced by lesion complexity, residual stenosis and restoration of post-procedure thrill.

OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the efficacy, feasibility, and safety of catheter-based interventional procedures for hypofunctioning haemodialysis fistulas in patients with CKD. METHODS: This single-centre, retrospective observational follow up study, enrolled with 100 CKD patients on maintenance haemodialysis with dysfunctional native arteriovenous fistulas who underwent fistulogram and catheter-based intervention.

title: Scleraxis regulates arterial smooth muscle phenotype to alter vascular stiffness.
abstract: Arterial stiffness impacts vessel function and may change due to alterations in wall components such as extracellular matrix (ECM) or vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs). Stiffening is associated with multiple cardiovascular diseases; thus, understanding its regulation is crucial for attenuating vessel pathology and function. We previously showed that scleraxis controls cardiac fibrosis-related gene expression, but its vascular role is unknown. Using a smooth muscle-specific scleraxis overexpression mouse model and angiotensin II (Ang II) minipump infusion, we measured mesenteric artery physical characteristics using pressure myography and assessed vessel structure by histology. We assessed the impact of scleraxis overexpression in human aortic smooth muscle cells (HAOSMCs). In vivo, scleraxis overexpression stimulated VSMC proliferation and increased mesenteric artery stiffness via a leftward shift of the stress versus strain curve. In vitro, scleraxis overexpression induced HAOSMC proliferation. Scleraxis knockout rightward shifted the mesentery stress versus strain curve. Ang II markedly increased scleraxis expression in coronary arteries. Scleraxis overexpression with Ang II infusion increased measures of mesentery stiffness, increased VSMC contractility, and impaired relaxation, while unexpectedly reducing ECM gene expression and increasing contractile gene expression and media/lumen ratio, suggesting arterial remodeling. Similarly, HAOSMCs infected with scleraxis and treated with Ang II demonstrated decreased proliferation and an increased contractile phenotype. Scleraxis expression in VSMCs is a novel regulator of vascular stiffness via altered proliferation, with its effect varying with Ang II presence. These findings reveal the first evidence of a role for scleraxis in vascular structure and function, highlighting its complex and context-dependent impact on vessel characteristics.NEW & NOTEWORTHY Scleraxis potently drives cardiac fibrosis, yet lacks any known function in the vasculature despite being highly upregulated in pathologies marked by increased vessel stiffness. Scleraxis overexpression in vascular smooth muscle cells in vivo increased their proliferation while also increasing measures of vascular stiffness. Scleraxis and angiotensin II together also increased stiffness, but this effect was related to increased contractile gene expression. This work provides the first description of scleraxis' role in the vasculature.

Stiffening is associated with multiple cardiovascular diseases; thus, understanding its regulation is crucial for attenuating vessel pathology and function. We previously showed that scleraxis controls cardiac fibrosis-related gene expression, but its vascular role is unknown.

title: Isolated Unilateral Proptosis as a Heralding Feature of Ipsilateral Temporal Dural Arteriovenous Fistula.
abstract: Dural arteriovenous fistulas (dAVFs) are rare intracranial vascular abnormalities that may present with varied and sometimes atypical clinical features. While proptosis is commonly associated with anterior cranial or cavernous sinus fistulas, it is unusual in posterior fossa dAVFs. We present the case of a 41-year-old man with progressive redness, swelling, and protrusion of the left eye over six months, without associated pain, diplopia, headache, or cranial nerve deficits. Ocular examination revealed preserved visual acuity and extraocular movements, with normal fundus findings. An initial diagnosis of a cavernous sinus fistula was considered. However, brain MRI with time-of-flight sequences revealed a left temporal dAVF with feeders from the external carotid artery and drainage into the vein of Labbé and transverse sinus, with a possible connection to the superior division of the middle cerebral artery. On clinical re-examination, a bruit was noted in the left occipitotemporal region. Doppler and transcranial Doppler studies confirmed mixed arterial and venous flow. The patient was referred for digital subtraction angiography and embolization. The symptoms of dAVFs vary depending on the shunt characteristics, location, and venous drainage pattern. Ocular signs are uncommon in noncavernous dAVFs. In this case, venous reflux through the vein of Labbé may explain the isolated proptosis. Management is guided by angioarchitecture and associated risk features, with high-risk fistulas requiring timely intervention. This case highlights the need to consider cranial dural AVFs in the differential diagnosis of isolated proptosis, as timely diagnosis and treatment are crucial.

title: Miniaturized piezoelectric tube actuated catheter (μPTAC) enabling distal actuation for intravascular optical coherence tomography.
abstract: Intravascular optical coherence tomography (IV-OCT) requires stable circumferential scanning, while long torque-transmission shafts can introduce non-uniform rotational distortion (NURD). This study presents a miniature piezoelectric tube-actuated catheter (μPTAC) that integrates a piezoelectric-tube stator, a gradient-index (GRIN) lens rotor, and a single-mode fiber for compact distal scanning. Two orthogonal bending modes excited with a 90° phase difference generate elliptical contact motion and friction-driven lens rotation. Finite element analysis and experimental characterization supported this actuation mechanism. The prototype incorporated a 4-mm-long tube with outer and inner diameters of 0.45 and 0.20 mm, respectively, exhibited a bending resonance at 68.68 kHz, and achieved a rotational speed of 2607 rpm under 50 Vpp excitation. A stationary mirror measurement yielded an axial full width at half maximum of 13.85 μm, while retrospective edge analysis gave an effective lateral width of approximately 34 μm. Analysis of selected vessel-wall images from the earlier and present probes yielded contrast-to-noise ratios (CNRs) of 0.53 ± 0.21 and 0.88 ± 0.17, respectively, and image-domain signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) proxies of 14.3 ± 4.2 and 19.4 ± 3.9 dB under their respective acquisition and processing conditions. Imaging experiments in air demonstrated three-dimensional phantom reconstruction, consistent feature placement, vascular-model navigation, and ex vivo imaging of a stented porcine coronary artery. These results support the integrated μPTAC architecture for compact distal IV-OCT scanning. Future work will focus on developing a distal piezoelectric ultrasonic motor actuator with improved rotational stability and reliability to enable clinical IV-OCT applications.

title: Increased Disarray of Extracellular Matrix Collagen-I Fiber Network and Compromised Biomechanics in Aortae From Marfan-Syndrome Mice Assessed Through Combined Opto-Biomechatronics.
abstract: Fibrillin‑1 (FBN1) mutations lead to extracellular matrix (ECM) defects with progressive aortic dilation in Marfan's syndrome (MFS). MFS thoracic aortas have increased stiffness, but how visco-elastic and microstructural abnormalities affect in vivo hemodynamics remains inconclusive. We applied ex vivo uniaxial visco-elasticity stress-relaxation testing and simultaneous 3D collagen Second Harmonic Generation (SHG) imaging to MFS and wt littermate linearized aortic strips with in vivo vascular function. MFS mouse (Fbn1mgR/mgR) aortas were stiffer and more viscous. SHG imaging revealed MFS ECM disorganization at rest and stronger collagen-alignment strain response than wt strips, indicating greater fibrillar straightening capacity. in vivo, MFS mice developed early, progressive aortic dilation. Pulse wave velocity was elevated in young MFS mice pre-dilation but declined as aneurysms formed. Female MFS aortic peak pressure and velocity were normal, but reduced in MFS-males vs. wt. Ex vivo perfused wt carotid arteries were highly compliant. Female MFS carotids were stiffer, had reduced radial strain, a right‑shifted pressure-strain curve and minimal wall‑thickness changes. MFS carotids did not recover baseline diameter after perfusion, indicating impaired visco-elastic recoil. We demonstrate early visco-elastic MFS aortic dysfunction and ECM disorder. Mechanistically, the larger collagen-straightening capacity in MFS cannot compensate for the increased visco-elasticity during a beat-to-beat cycle.

title: Adipose-derived microRNA-518a drives hepatic cholesterol dysregulation and hypertension-related vascular remodeling in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis via the MST1-AMPK-SREBP2 axis.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is characterized by disrupted hepatic lipid homeostasis and progressive liver injury, and frequently coexists with hypertension and systemic vascular remodeling, suggesting shared pathophysiological mechanisms. Although adipose tissue-derived microRNAs have emerged as important mediators of inter-organ communication, their roles in regulating hepatic cholesterol metabolism and vascular dysfunction during MASH remain incompletely understood.

OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate whether microRNA-518a regulates hepatic cholesterol metabolism and MASH progression through the MST1-AMPK-SREBP2 signaling pathway and to explore its potential implications for vascular remodeling and hypertension.

METHODS: Integrative bioinformatic analyses, including Mendelian randomization and transcriptomic network analysis, were performed to identify candidate regulatory pathways associated with MASH. Functional validation was conducted using human clinical samples, in vitro cell models, exosome-mediated microRNA delivery, and a dietary mouse model of MASH.

RESULTS: MST1 was identified as a key regulatory target of microRNA-518a. Increased microRNA-518a expression suppressed MST1, resulting in reduced AMPK activation and enhanced SREBP2-mediated cholesterol biosynthesis. Functional experiments demonstrated that microRNA-518a promoted hepatic cholesterol accumulation, lipid deposition, inflammation, and fibrotic changes, whereas restoration of MST1 partially reversed these effects. Exosome-mediated delivery of microRNA-518a further supported its ability to modulate hepatic metabolic responses through intercellular communication.

CONCLUSIONS: MicroRNA-518a promotes hepatic cholesterol dysregulation and MASH progression by targeting the MST1-AMPK-SREBP2 signaling pathway. Notably, the convergence of this axis with vascular regulatory networks suggests broader implications for understanding the metabolic-vascular comorbidities frequently observed in MASH patients, including hypertension and arterial stiffness.

Although adipose tissue-derived microRNAs have emerged as important mediators of inter-organ communication, their roles in regulating hepatic cholesterol metabolism and vascular dysfunction during MASH remain incompletely understood. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to investigate whether microRNA-518a regulates hepatic cholesterol metabolism and MASH progression through the MST1-AMPK-SREBP2 signaling pathway and to explore its potential implications for vascular remodeling and hypertension.

title: Follistatin Alleviates Vascular Dysfunction by Reducing Oxidative Stress and Promoting Browning in Perivascular Adipose Tissue.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Essential hypertension, characterized by vascular dysfunction, remains a leading modifiable cause of death globally. Perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT), which normally reduces vasoconstriction, becomes contractile in hypertension due to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS). Brown PVAT has emerged as a protective regulator of vascular tone. Follistatin, an activin antagonist, induces adipose tissue browning via AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase). We recently reported improved blood pressure and vascular function by follistatin in the spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR) model of essential hypertension. Here, we investigate whether follistatin reduces ROS and induces browning in SHR PVAT to restore PVAT-mediated vascular function.

METHODS: SHRs were treated with vehicle, follistatin, or hydralazine for 8 weeks. Mesenteric white and thoracic brown PVAT from SHR and normotensive Wistar-Kyoto mice were used, with wire myography used to assess vascular function. PVAT nitric oxide, ROS, and browning markers were assessed via immunohistochemistry. PVAT was treated ex vivo to assess mechanisms of browning. Unbiased proteomic analysis of PVAT was performed using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry.

RESULTS: SHR PVAT dysfunction, manifesting as a procontractile effect, was inhibited by follistatin through reducing ROS, enhancing NO bioavailability, and promoting browning. These effects were mediated by activin neutralization and AMPK phosphorylation. Hydralazine-induced blood pressure reduction did not replicate follistatin effects, suggesting vascular benefits of follistatin are mediated by direct PVAT modulation. Proteomic analysis revealed a shift in proteome towards a normal state, upregulating processes associated with adipose browning.

CONCLUSIONS: Follistatin restores PVAT-mediated vascular relaxation via ROS reduction, activin neutralization, and AMPK-dependent browning, positioning the potential for PVAT as a therapeutic target for vascular dysfunction in essential hypertension.

Perivascular adipose tissue (PVAT), which normally reduces vasoconstriction, becomes contractile in hypertension due to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS). title: Chronic traumatic popliteal arteriovenous fistula presenting twenty years after shotgun injury: a case report and critical literature review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Traumatic arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs) account for only 2.5-4% of penetrating vascular injuries, yet their natural history is insidious: most remain hemodynamically compensated for years before clinical decompensation. Delayed popliteal AVF poses unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges because of the anatomically confined surgical field, proximity of neurovascular structures, and historical amputation rates of 10-20%. This report is prepared in accordance with the CARE criteria for case reports.

CASE PRESENTATION: A 64-year-old male smoker presented with a 10-day history of progressive left popliteal pain and a pulsatile mass, precisely 20 years after conservative management of a shotgun injury to the same limb. Physical examination revealed a continuous machinery-type bruit and thrill. CT angiography confirmed a direct popliteal arteriovenous communication, a 25 mm secondary venous aneurysm, proximal arterial dilation to 16 mm, and-critically-incidental cardiomegaly with ascending aortic dilation (44 mm), may reflect chronic systemic high-output circulatory adaptation secondary to AV shunting. Open surgical repair with fistula ligation and aneurysmorrhaphy was performed.

DISCUSSION: This case exemplifies the full natural history of a chronic traumatic AVF: prolonged asymptomatic compensation, progressive vascular remodeling, venous aneurysm formation, and systemic cardiac adaptation. We present an analysis of pathophysiology, diagnostic modalities, and evidence-based treatment selection alongside a proposed five-step management algorithm.

CONCLUSION: Traumatic popliteal AVF can remain silent for decades. The coexistence of venous aneurysm, chronic cardiac remodeling, and 20-year-old scar tissue argues for individualized management guided by echocardiographic hemodynamics and anatomic complexity.

Delayed popliteal AVF poses unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges because of the anatomically confined surgical field, proximity of neurovascular structures, and historical amputation rates of 10-20%. title: Chronic fructose intake disrupts extracellular ATP-pyrophosphate homeostasis and increases susceptibility to aortic calcification.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Excessive fructose consumption has become increasingly prevalent in modern diets and is strongly associated with metabolic disorders and elevated cardiovascular risk. Vascular calcification, a major contributor to arterial stiffness, is regulated by the balance between pro-calcifying factors and endogenous calcification inhibitors such as extracellular inorganic pyrophosphate. However, the effects of chronic fructose intake on pyrophosphate homeostasis, as well as their contribution to vascular calcification, remain incompletely understood.

METHODS: Male Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to a 10% fructose-enriched drinking solution for three months. Metabolic, biochemical, and vascular parameters were assessed, including plasma glucose, insulin, inflammatory cytokines, uric acid, mineral metabolism markers, ATP and pyrophosphate levels, hepatic mitochondrial function, and aortic calcification. Extracellular pyrophosphate metabolism in the aortic wall was evaluated, and the effects of genetic or pharmacological dual inhibition of TNAP and eNTPD1 on vascular calcification were examined ex vivo.

RESULTS: Fructose-fed rats developed hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, elevated inflammatory cytokines, and increased uric acid levels despite unchanged body weight. They also exhibited increased plasma calcium and reduced 25-OH vitamin D levels without changes in phosphate or magnesium concentrations. Plasma ATP and pyrophosphate levels were significantly reduced, indicating impaired systemic anti-calcifying capacity. High fructose intake induced marked hepatic mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by reduced ATP synthesis, increased H₂O₂ production, decreased mitochondrial membrane potential, impaired respiratory chain activity, and reduced oxygen consumption. In the aorta, fructose feeding increased calcification, decreased extracellular pyrophosphate synthesis, and enhanced pyrophosphate degradation. Dual inhibition of TNAP and eNTPD1 significantly reduced aortic calcification ex vivo, supporting the role of pyrophosphate-regulating enzymes in fructose-induced vascular mineralization.

CONCLUSION: These findings show that chronic fructose intake disrupts both systemic and local pyrophosphate homeostasis promoting a pro-calcifying environment. Targeting pyrophosphate-regulating pathways may represent a therapeutic strategy to prevent fructose-associated aortic calcification.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Excessive fructose consumption has become increasingly prevalent in modern diets and is strongly associated with metabolic disorders and elevated cardiovascular risk. Vascular calcification, a major contributor to arterial stiffness, is regulated by the balance between pro-calcifying factors and endogenous calcification inhibitors such as extracellular inorganic pyrophosphate. However, the effects of chronic fructose intake on pyrophosphate homeostasis, as well as their contribution to vascular calcification, remain incompletely understood.

title: Pericyte KATP channel hyperactivity redistributes cortical blood flow in a CADASIL mouse model.
abstract: Cerebral hemodynamic dysfunction is a key driver of unhealthy brain aging. Impaired microcirculatory reactivity leads to uneven perfusion, rendering deeper brain regions more vulnerable and thereby contributing to cognitive decline. Yet how capillaries contribute to these deficits remains poorly defined. Here we combined spatial transcriptomics with in vivo two-photon and three-photon imaging to measure layer-specific cerebral blood flow in control and small vessel disease model mice (CADASIL TgNotch3R169C). We found downregulation of ATP-synthesizing genes, indicating microvascular metabolic impairment that paralleled impaired pericyte bioenergetics. This energy deficit coincided with diminished tone in the arteriole-capillary transitional zone and reduced deep-layer perfusion. Complementary electrophysiology, ex vivo and in silico approaches, revealed that hyperactive KATP channels in pericytes drive a redistribution of cerebral blood flow toward superficial cortical layers. This loss of spatial perfusion equalization, despite preserved global flow, contributed to deep-layer hypoperfusion, establishing a previously underrecognized but tractable vascular function disrupted in aging pathology.

title: IgA-enriched phenotype predicts liver-related events in MASLD.
abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a complex, multifactorial condition. To achieve truly personalized therapy for MASLD, it will be essential to stratify patients based on clinical and biochemical data by identifying subgroups with distinct disease mechanisms and prognostic trajectories.

METHODS: This study conducted unbiased clustering analysis of 349 patients with MASLD based on clinical variables. Multi-omics analyses that included spatial transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and immunohistochemistry were subsequently applied to characterize the biological features of high-risk subgroups.

RESULTS: Among the four identified MASLD subgroups, one cluster showed a higher 5-year cumulative incidence of liver-related events (LREs) (24.0%; 95% CI 14.8%-37.4%), with excess risk persisting after adjustment for advanced fibrosis. This high-risk subgroup was characterized by an immune-driven disease phenotype with excessive immunoglobulin A (IgA) expression. Multivariable analysis identified elevated IgA (≥318 mg/dl) as an independent predictor of LREs (hazard ratio = 3.17, 95% CI 1.27-7.91; p = 0.01), a finding validated in an independent vibration-controlled transient elastography cohort (n = 287) as well as an external multicenter validation cohort (n = 272). Spatial transcriptomics and scRNA-seq analyses demonstrated portal enrichment of IgA-expressing B-lineage cells, with IGHA1-high regions showing activation of pathways related to B-cell receptor signaling, extracellular matrix remodeling, and vascular remodeling. Intestinal immunohistochemistry and circulating EndoCAb IgG levels supported a link between increased gut permeability and coordinated systemic and intrahepatic IgA-associated immune activation.

CONCLUSION: A data-driven clustering strategy identified a novel MASLD subtype characterized by enhanced IgA-mediated immune activation along the gut-liver axis as a key determinant of disease progression. This IgA-based stratification improves risk assessment and enables mechanism-based therapeutic targeting in patients with high-risk MASLD.

IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: This study identified a high-risk MASLD subgroup characterized by elevated IgA levels and increased incidence of liver-related events, independent of fibrosis severity. These findings highlight the relevance of immune dysregulation, particularly IgA-associated responses, in MASLD progression.

To achieve truly personalized therapy for MASLD, it will be essential to stratify patients based on clinical and biochemical data by identifying subgroups with distinct disease mechanisms and prognostic trajectories. METHODS: This study conducted unbiased clustering analysis of 349 patients with MASLD based on clinical variables.

title: Proteostasis is disrupted in human endothelial cells by serum from ATTR patients and is rescued by tafamidis treatment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The vascular effects of wild-type (ATTRwt-CM) and hereditary (ATTRv-CM) transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, and the impact of tafamidis treatment, remain unclear.

METHODS: Serum from ATTRwt-CM and ATTRv-CM patients (pre- and 6-months post-Tafamidis treatment) elderly and young controls, was applied on human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Viability, motility, and stress responses and serum cytokine and proteomic profiles were assessed. Recombinant TTR, with and without tafamidis co-treatment, were also evaluated. Pulse wave velocity (PWV) was longitudinally assessed in ATTRwt-CM patients pre- and post-tafamidis treatment and in elderly controls.

RESULTS: ATTRwt-CM or ATTRv serum reduced HUVECs viability and motility, inducing proteotoxic and oxidative stress, while serum cytokine and proteome profiling revealed inflammatory-related signatures; All these effects were attenuated in HUVECs treated with post-Tafamidis serum. Recombinant TTR also induced proteotoxic stress, which was attenuated by tafamidis co-treatment (safety range ≤ 16 μM). Consistently, PWV was reduced in ATTRwt-CM patients after Tafamidis, as compared to controls, correlating with increased serum transthyretin and reduced PBMCs' proteasome activity.

CONCLUSIONS: Serum from ATTR-CM patients or recombinant TTR directly induced toxic effects in HUVECs. Tafamidis mitigated these effects in vitro and improved arterial stiffness in ATTRwt-CM patients, implying protective vascular effects of tafamidis in ATTR-CM beyond direct myocardial transthyretin stabilization.

METHODS: Serum from ATTRwt-CM and ATTRv-CM patients (pre- and 6-months post-Tafamidis treatment) elderly and young controls, was applied on human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs). Viability, motility, and stress responses and serum cytokine and proteomic profiles were assessed.

title: Endothelial dysfunction in aging associated with reduced Niban phosphorylation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of mortality worldwide, with aging and endothelial dysfunction being key contributors to its progression. Age-related vascular dysfunction is characterized by impaired endothelial-dependent relaxation, increased vascular inflammation, and heightened susceptibility to injury, all of which exacerbate cardiovascular risk. The multi-functional protein Niban restores vascular function following injury, with reduced Niban phosphorylation linked to activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways. We hypothesized that reduced Niban phosphorylation and increased inflammatory MAPK signaling would be associated with vascular dysfunction in aging that can be attenuated by NiPp, a cell permeant phosphomimetic peptide of Niban. METHODS AND RESULTS: Aortas from young (3-months-old, N = 8) and aged (20- to 23-month-old N = 8) rats were assessed for vascular reactivity as well as protein levels and protein phosphorylation. Aged aortas displayed impaired contractility, endothelial-dependent relaxation, reduced phosphorylated Niban levels, and increased phosphorylation of inflammatory MAPK pathway elements including c-Jun N-terminal kinase, MAP kinase-activated protein kinase 2, phosphorylated cAMP response element-binding protein, and downstream vascular cell adhesion molecule-1. Aged aortas also exhibited greater IL-1β-induced loss of endothelial-dependent relaxation ex vivo, which was attenuated by NiPp treatment. CONCLUSION: These results identify reduced Niban phosphorylation and increased MAPK signaling as contributors to age-related endothelial dysfunction and highlight Niban phosphorylation as a possible target for treating vascular aging and associated cardiovascular diseases.

Age-related vascular dysfunction is characterized by impaired endothelial-dependent relaxation, increased vascular inflammation, and heightened susceptibility to injury, all of which exacerbate cardiovascular risk. The multi-functional protein Niban restores vascular function following injury, with reduced Niban phosphorylation linked to activation of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways.

title: Brown adipose tissue-derived exosomes ameliorate obesity-related hypertension via HuR-mediated restoration of endothelial function.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Obesity-related hypertension (OH) is driven by endothelial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and oxidative stress, yet effective targeted therapies are lacking. This study aims to investigate the mechanisms by which brown adipose tissue-derived exosomes (BAT-Exos) improve vascular endothelial function in OH via HuR protein delivery.

METHODS: Rat models with OH and palmitic acid-treated endothelial cell injury models were established. BAT-Exos were compared with white adipose tissue-derived exosomes (WAT-Exos) for therapeutic efficacy. In vitro, primary endothelial cells isolated from rat aortas were treated with palmitic acid to induce injury, followed by pre-treatment with BAT-Exos or WAT-Exos. Inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, oxidative stress markers, eNOS activity, and nitric oxide (NO) levels were measured.

RESULTS: BAT-Exos exert superior therapeutic effects compared to WAT-Exos in both in vivo and in vitro models of OH. In rat model of high-fat-diet-induced OH, BAT-Exos improved metabolic profiles, lowered blood pressure, and alleviated vascular remodeling, while reducing inflammation and restoring eNOS activity. In vitro, BAT-Exos significantly mitigated palmitic acid-induced endothelial dysfunction by suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules, and oxidative stress markers, while enhancing nitric oxide production.

CONCLUSION: These findings confirm HuR as a key therapeutic cargo. The BAT-Exo-HuR axis represents a novel intercellular signaling pathway that improves vascular function and may serve as a promising strategy for treating OH and related cardiovascular disorders.

This study aims to investigate the mechanisms by which brown adipose tissue-derived exosomes (BAT-Exos) improve vascular endothelial function in OH via HuR protein delivery. METHODS: Rat models with OH and palmitic acid-treated endothelial cell injury models were established.

title: Far-infrared irradiation attenuates vessel contraction by activating SERCA2 through disruption of SERCA2 and PLN interaction.
abstract: Vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) plays an important role in maintaining vascular function by responding to various vasoactive stimuli within blood vessels. Far-infrared (FIR) rays has been shown to possess a variety of physiological effects including vasodilation, while the underlying molecular mechanism remains elusive. Here, we explored the molecular mechanism by which FIR irradiation suppresses vascular contraction using rat VSMCs and aortas. FIR irradiation enhanced the transport of intracellular Ca2+ from the cytosol to the sarcoendoplasmic reticulum (SER) via activation of sarcoendoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA), which accompanied a decrease in intracellular ATP levels. Pretreatment with thapsigargin (TG), a specific SERCA inhibitor, or knockdown of SERCA2 gene expression reversed FIR irradiation-induced translocation of Ca2+ into the SER. Notably, FIR irradiation promoted the dissociation of SERCA2 and phospholamban (PLN), an endogenous SERCA inhibitor, without altering their total protein expression levels. The array of effects elicited by FIR irradiation was not observed under hyperthermic conditions (39°C). Moreover, FIR irradiation, but not hyperthermal condition, decreased the phosphorylation of myosin light chain (MLC) at Ser19, which was restored by pretreatment with TG or the knockdown of SERCA2 gene expression. FIR irradiation attenuated phenylephrine-induced vessel contraction in endothelium-deprived rat aortas. Consistent with the in vitro results, the reduction in MLC phosphorylation caused by FIR irradiation was reversed following pretreatment with TG in isolated aortas. Additionally, FIR irradiation increased blood flow in the carotid arteries of mice. Collectively, these results suggest that FIR irradiation activates SERCA2 by promoting its dissociation from PLN, independent of hyperthermic effects. This activation lowers cytosolic Ca²⁺ and ATP levels, reducing MLC phosphorylation and vascular smooth muscle contraction. These findings provide scientific evidence for the therapeutic potential of FIR therapy in the treatment and prevention of arterial narrowing conditions such as pathological vasospasm, and peripheral artery disease.

Here, we explored the molecular mechanism by which FIR irradiation suppresses vascular contraction using rat VSMCs and aortas.

title: Autonomic dysfunction and vasoregulation in long COVID-19 are linked to anti-GPCR autoantibodies.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2-triggered autoantibodies (AABs) targeting G protein-coupled receptors have been suggested to contribute to the post-acute sequelae of coronavirus disease 2019 (or post-COVID-19 syndrome [PCS]).

OBJECTIVE: We sought to characterize AABs involved in autonomic dysfunction such as rhythm control and vasoregulation in patients with PCS and profile the peripheral B- and T-cell receptor (BCR/TCR) architecture to identify immunogenetic imprints of autoimmunity.

METHODS: Anti-G protein-coupled receptor AABs were characterized in patients with PCS with known alteration in autonomic nervous system functions assessed by heart rate variability. Adaptive immune receptor repertoire sequencing was used to profile peripheral BCR and TCR architecture. Patients with COVID-19 with severe or moderate acute disease, after recovery, and prepandemic healthy individuals served as controls. Cardio- and vasoactive effects of AABs were analyzed using 24-hour and exercise test blood pressure measurements. The direct effect of AABs on electromechanical coupling was tested in human-induced pluripotent stem cell cardiomyocytes.

RESULTS: AABs including autoantibody against angiotensin II receptor type 1/2, autoantibody against adrenoceptor beta 1/2, autoantibody against muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M1/M3, and autoantibody against C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (CXCR3ab) were associated with heart rate variability alterations. Analysis of the broad BCR repertoire metrics revealed high similarity between patients with PCS and healthy controls for clonality and diversity measures. The level of somatic hypermutation as proxy for antigen experience was equal to that of healthy controls. Elevated CXCR3ab levels were linked to higher 24-hour mean arterial pressure, whereas patients with elevated autoantibody against muscarinic acetylcholine receptor M1 and CXCR3ab levels showed higher blood pressure during stress tests. AABs had no effect on beat frequency and amplitude of cardiomyocyte contraction in vitro.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that AABs play a modulatory role in sympathetic nervous system-mediated regulation of cardiac rhythm and vascular function in PCS. AAB levels did not correlate with BCR and TCR repertoire metrics or T-cell receptor beta variable gene usage.

title: Piezo-type mechanosensitive ion channel component 1 (PIEZO1) is upregulated in peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and a novel murine PAD model.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The objectives of this work are to: define murine femoral artery stiffening with age and the modifiability of this process by exercise; impose peripheral arterial disease (PAD) hemodynamics on murine femoral arteries and to deliver focal atherosclerotic plaque to femoral arteries; and test piezo-type mechanosensitive ion channel component 1 (PIEZO1) expression in human and murine femoral arteries of PAD.

METHODS: We used a running wheel to exercise young and old S129 mice and biomechanical testing to quantify changes in arterial stiffness. We created a novel partial femoral artery ligation (PFL) model to impose PAD hemodynamics via low wall shear stress (WSS) to create a flow-mediated model of arterial aging in femoral arteries. In vivo mechanics were defined with ultrasound. Ex vivo arteries underwent biaxial tests. Atherogenic conditions were induced using PCSK9 infection and a high-fat diet. Arterial remodeling and PIEZO1 expression were quantified by histology.

RESULTS: Femoral arteries are naturally stiffer than carotid arteries; both stiffen further with aging, but exercise improved compliance in old femoral arteries. PFL imposed low WSS and stiffening, similar to that seen in aging. Under atherogenic conditions, PFL delivered focal atherosclerotic plaques in femoral arteries. Low WSS increased PIEZO1 expression in femoral arteries (∼1.8× in endothelial cells, ∼2.4× in smooth muscle cells, and ∼2.8× in macrophages). Human PAD arteries with high-grade stenosis validated increased PIEZO1 mRNA (∼1.83×).

CONCLUSIONS: Femoral artery mechanics differ significantly from the carotid artery but can be modified by exercise. This PFL model confers arterial stiffness, and under atherogenic conditions, delivers focal femoral atherosclerotic plaque. PIEZO1 expression increases in both PFL-treated mouse femoral arteries and human PAD arteries with severe stenosis, supporting this as a translational target for PAD.

CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is the third most common atherosclerotic bed. PAD is associated with increased risk of limb loss and death, but the mechanisms driving site-specific arterial remodeling in PAD remain unclear. This work uniquely creates a model of PAD that incorporates arterial stiffening via aging and flow disturbances and inducing atherosclerotic plaque into the murine femoral artery. By comparing murine femoral arteries with PAD arteries, piezo-type mechanosensitive ion channel component 1 (PIEZO1) was discovered as key mediator linking PAD blood flow and stiffening to untoward changes in endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, and macrophages within femoral arteries. Targeted modulation of PIEZO1 activity provide PAD-centric therapeutic strategies and help promote the vascular health, life, and limb outcomes in patients with PAD.
